chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Phrasing across bar lines before Charlie Parker: Don Redman
summary: Asked who phrased unusually before Parker, Horace names Don Redman for anticipating bars and out-of-key breaks, before Bird and Dizzy took it further.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Did you ever know of

anybody that was really getting into unusual phrasing? Of course, Louis did quite a lot, but we often think of the very unusual kind of phrasing coming in with Charlie Parker pretty much; that is, you know, carrying phrases longer than the four bars and then beginning the next phrase in the middle of what the usual phrase ought to be, that sort of thing. Do you recall any players that were doing that at all?
Earlier than Charlie -- that's a good question, Tom. I don't recall offhand. Let's see. You say earlier than Charlie.
Yeah, this would be like late '30's or even the very early '40's.

I know there were a lot of musicians that would anticipate the progression over into the next bar; they would carry them over. And like the first guy, I think, that used to do that was Don Redman, the great alto saxophonist and arranger, in years. In fact, Don used to make a lot of out of key breaks and come back into the tonic, you know. And he'd experiment. And it would work. And he'd anticipate the moving to the next bar. But he'd always know how to catch up and where to do it, you know, and then I would know some other guys that weren't quite as fortunate, because you had to know your horn in order to do those things, you know. So I
hope this answers part of your question anyway.
In a way, yes. Well, I was just tossing it out there.
And, of course, the great Bird came on and did it up.
He did start something together, though, and Dizzy didn't they?
